title: Sixteen showings (1373)
hookLine: near death at thirty, Julian sees sixteen visions of Christ
tomorrow: she waited years to learn what it all meant. what was the answer?

cards: Anyone who has had a bad fever knows the ceiling can do strange things. So when a woman everyone thinks is dying says she saw something, the obvious question arrives fast. The curate sets a crucifix before her face.
Her sight fails, she writes, and the room goes dark as night, except the cross, which keeps an ordinary light. Then she sees red blood trickling down under the crown of thorns.
Julian of Norwich calls it the first of sixteen showings. Fever, or gift?

teach.b: Start with what she tells us.
Earlier in life, Julian writes, she prayed for three gifts: a vivid mind of Christ's suffering, a bodily sickness, and three wounds, which she names contrition, compassion and longing for God.
When she was thirty and a half, the sickness came, and she thought she would die. The text dates the showings to May of 1373, and her book counts sixteen. Now the two Catholic readings.

The first takes the showings as she did: given by God, worth a lifetime of pondering. She calls them showings, not dreams, and builds her whole book on them. The second is careful, and it starts inside her own story.

teach.h: VIEW TWO: SHE SAID SHE HAD RAVED.
teach.b: Once she recovered, a religious man asked how she was, and she told him she had raved that day. Then she mentioned the bleeding cross, and he grew serious, and she was ashamed she'd brushed it off.
The Catechism says private revelations, even ones the Church recognizes, don't belong to the deposit of faith; their role is to help people live the faith more fully.
So a Catholic may treasure Julian's visions, or hold that question open and still read her for what she teaches. Both readers end up doing the same thing: reading her slowly.

how: Catholics read Julian's Revelations of Divine Love as a classic of prayer; the Church teaches that private revelations, even recognized ones, are not part of the deposit of faith, so belief in them is not required.

games.q: you've always heard that a vision is either straight from God or nonsense. state the careful Catholic reading of Julian at its strongest.
o: visions are never from God, so Catholics simply ignore them.
private revelations aren't required belief, but can help someone live the faith; read Julian for what she teaches.
only priests are allowed to read books about private revelations.
games.why: the Catechism leaves room: private revelations don't belong to the deposit of faith, and their role is to help people live it. Julian herself once wondered.

practice: Find a pen and any scrap of paper. Write one line by hand about a moment from the last day or two that, looking back, felt like a gift: a word, a meal, a face. Then rest with that line in front of you for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: Sixteen showings. Julian's word for what she was given to see on her sickbed, beginning with the cross.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: sixteen showings, and a woman who wrote down every one. More tomorrow.
